candidates.statement: This guidance recommends best practices for sponsors considering proprietary names for 33 nonprescription drugs and is intended to provide sponsors clarity and transparency with respect 34 to the factors and framework FDA uses to evaluate proposed proprietary names for 35 nonprescription drugs that are subject to premarket review. Use of the best practice 36 recommendations and other assessment tools addressed in this guidance is not mandatory, and 37 their application does not dictate specific outcomes. Assessments of a proprietary name are 38 necessarily fact-specific and thus, where FDA makes a determination about the acceptance of a 39 proprietary name for a nonprescription drug as part of the new drug approval process, it does so 40 on a case-by-case basis, considering the totality of the information. 41 In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 42 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 43 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 44 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 45 not required. 46

candidates.statement: II. BACKGROUND 47 Selecting a proprietary name is a critical element in drug product design and development 48 because end users may rely, in part or in whole, on the proprietary name to identify which 49 product, among thousands of available products, is intended for or used by a particular person. 50 Nonprescription drug product proprietary names are used by consumers, patients, caregivers, 51 physicians and other health care professionals as primary product identifiers. Having a 52 proprietary name that facilitates accurate identification of a nonprescription drug product by 53 these end users is critical for its safe and effective use. For example, if end users cannot easily 54 identify a nonprescription product or distinguish a proprietary name from other drug names that 55 are similar phonetically (sound-alike names) or in their spelling or orthographic appearance 56 (look-alike names), or if the drug name is otherwise confusing or misleading, the end user might 57 select or receive the wrong product or it might not be possible to correctly identify the product 58 used. Using best practices for selecting a proprietary name for a nonprescription drug helps 59 minimize these hazards, which in turn both promotes public health and helps to ensure that the 60 product conforms to legal requirements under the FD&C Act. 61 To inform their risk assessment of a proposed nonprescription product proprietary name, 62 sponsors should consider how their nonprescription product will be used by consumers, patients, 63 caregivers, physicians and other health care professionals. 64

candidates.statement: 12/07/20 4 certain considerations that shall be considered when determining whether labeling is misleading. 92 FDA regulations also address some of the ways in which the name of a drug may render its 93 labeling misleading. 16 In addition, labeling is relevant to determining whether a drug is a new 94 drug under section 201(p) of the FD&C Act that requires premarket approval (see sections 95 505(a) and 301(d) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 355(a) and 331(d)). 96 For nonprescription products that will be marketed under an NDA, ANDA, or BLA, FDA 97 reviews proposed labeling, including any proposed proprietary name included in that labeling, on 98 a case-by-case basis as part of the application review process. Although the Prescription Drug 99 User Fee Act (PDUFA) and Biosimilar User Fee Act (BsUFA) performance goals provide for 100 FDA to make a tentative determination of acceptance/non-acceptance of a proposed proprietary 101 name early in the review process (in instances where the proprietary name review request is 102 submitted as a complete submission), final acceptance of a proposed proprietary name occurs as 103 part of the approval of the drug product. 17 To reach that conclusion, in addition to considering 104 the safety and effectiveness data submitted to support approval, FDA considers the information 105 and analyses about the proposed proprietary name described in this guidance, along with any 106 additional proprietary name-related information submitted by the sponsor. In these cases, FDA’s 107 evaluation process is very similar to that which it uses to review proposed proprietary names for 108 prescription drug products. 109

candidates.statement: 12/07/20 5 proprietary name causes or contributes to medication errors, the sponsor of that product should 125 work expeditiously with FDA to resolve the situation. If the product does not comply with 126 applicable requirements, and the sponsor is unwilling to address or resolve an issue voluntarily, 127 the sponsor and/or the product may be subject to enforcement or regulatory actions. 128 This guidance is organized as follows: 129  Section III provides recommendations for developing and evaluating novel proprietary 130 names for nonprescription drug products. 131  Section IV describes FDA’s current thinking on the use of a proprietary name that is 132 already associated with a marketed product(s) to introduce a new product. 133  Section V provides recommendations for proprietary names for products that change 134 from prescription to nonprescription drug status. 135 For each category, we believe that no single test or standard is adequate to determine whether a 136 proposed proprietary name may contribute to errors or otherwise contribute to any violation of 137 the FD&C Act. Rather, the current approach to proposed proprietary name evaluation uses a 138 combination of different and complementary tests. 139

candidates.statement: 1. Names That Include Reference to Product-Specific Attributes 163 For flexibility in future product development and naming, FDA recommends that sponsors avoid 164 incorporating product-specific attributes, such as dosage form (e.g. “Name tabs ”) or route of 165 administration (e.g. “Name oral ”), as part of the proposed root proprietary name . It is not 166 uncommon for product-specific attributes to change during a drug’s life cycle with subsequent 167 introductions of new dosing intervals, formulations, dosage forms, indications, and patient 168 populations. If considering a proprietary name that includes or refers to product-specific 169 attributes, sponsors should be mindful that future changes, such as changes in dosage form or 170 route of administration, could render the root proprietary name inaccurate and thus unusable for 171 future formulations. 172 If references to product-specific attributes are included in the root proprietary name, FDA 173 recommends that the name be evaluated to ensure that the product-specific attribute is consistent 174 with the terminology used in the product’s labeling and does not pose risks for medication error. 175

Medical Abbreviations 176 Sponsors are generally discouraged from incorporating symbols, dose designations, and medical 177 abbreviations commonly used for prescription communication in their proposed proprietary 178 name because their inclusion could inadvertently introduce a source of error. Although we 179 acknowledge that consumers may not be familiar with these elements, health care providers 180 interact with nonprescription drug product proprietary names in a variety of health care settings 181 (see section II) and thus, inclusion of these elements in a nonprescription proprietary name can 182 contribute to confusion among these end users. 183 We recommend consulting The Joint Commission’s “Do Not Use” list or the Institute for Safe 184 Medication Practices (ISMP) List of Error-Prone Abbreviations, Symbols, and Dose 185 Designations when considering the risk that a proposed pro

candidates.statement: 12/07/20 9 drug product’s proprietary name. For these reasons, FDA believes it would be useful for 271 sponsors to conduct more comprehensive simulation studies. 272 Generally, name simulation studies test how subjects respond to a proposed proprietary name by 273 asking subjects to use the name in conditions that simulate the real world. The more closely and 274 fully the simulation approximates real-world use conditions, the more generalizable the results of 275 the simulation testing. Name simulation tasks should reflect the full range and variety of tasks 276 involved in the use of nonprescription drug products. Nonprescription products are often 277 selected, purchased, and used by consumers without the oversight of a health care professional. 278 Additionally, as noted in section II above, nonprescription products may be prescribed, ordered, 279 transcribed, dispensed, or administered by health care professionals using a proprietary name in a 280 variety of health care settings. 23 Therefore, it is important to evaluate whether all end users, 281 including consumers and health care professionals, can interpret both written and oral 282 communications of the proposed proprietary name. Thus, sponsors should design name 283 simulation studies for nonprescription product proprietary names to test how consumers and 284 health care professionals respond to the proposed name. FDA recommends that sponsors that 285 conduct such simulation studies consider the study design principles provided in Appendix C of 286 guidance for industry Best Practices in Developing Proprietary Names for Human Prescription 287 Drug Products . 288
